analysis.one_liner: Sends $100 billion in federal grants and bonds to repair and modernize public school buildings, prioritizing high-poverty districts.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on July 27, 2023, drew 23 Democratic cosponsors, and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would authorize $20 billion a year for five years in grants to states, awarded competitively to school districts serving the most low-income students, for repairs like fixing heating and ventilation, improving indoor air quality, removing lead and other toxins, and making buildings accessible to people with disabilities. It would also restore federal tax-credit bonds that let school districts borrow for construction at sharply reduced cost, set aside money for school foundations damaged by pyrrhotite, and increase construction funding for districts that serve military families and federally connected students. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and staff at public schools in low-income districts, which would get priority for repair and modernization grants; districts with weak ability to raise their own construction money through property taxes or bonds; construction workers, who would be covered by federal prevailing-wage standards on bond-financed projects; and American manufacturers of iron, steel, and construction products, which projects must use.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a need-based grant program directing money to districts with the most low-income students, the least capacity to raise construction funds, and the worst building conditions, with priority to schools where 40% or more of elementary and middle school students qualify for free or reduced-price lunch.

Funds repairs for specific health and safety problems: major repairs and deferred maintenance, indoor air quality, removal of lead, asbestos, and other toxic substances, safe drinking water testing, and accessibility for people with disabilities.

Restores school infrastructure tax credit bonds — a financing tool in which the federal government effectively covers the interest on district construction borrowing — capped at $10 billion a year, allocated by states using the same low-income priorities as the grant program.

Requires federal prevailing-wage labor standards on bond-financed projects and requires projects to use American iron, steel, and manufactured products, with waivers only under narrow conditions such as a cost increase over 25%.

Establishes a separate grant program, funded 50% federal and 40% state, to repair or replace school concrete foundations crumbling from pyrrhotite, and raises Impact Aid construction funding to $100 million a year for districts serving federally connected students.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund the $20 billion annual grant authorization and the forgone federal revenue on the tax-credit bonds; state governments, which must put up a 10% match from non-federal sources and keep their own school construction spending from falling; and, indirectly, project budgets, because Buy America and green-building certification requirements can raise construction costs.

drawbacks.text: The authorization totals $100 billion over five years ($20 billion a year for fiscal years 2024 through 2028) on top of $10 billion a year in tax-credit bond authority, a large new federal commitment that would eventually fall on taxpayers.

States must contribute a 10% non-federal match (though the match is waived in any year appropriations exceed $7 billion), which can strain state budgets and give poorer states less access to the program.

Requiring green-building certification (such as LEED), modern energy codes, and domestic iron, steel, and manufactured products can raise the cost of each project — the bill itself allows a Buy America waiver if domestic sourcing would raise project costs by more than 25%.

The bill bars use of any funds for facilities of for-profit charter schools or charter schools leasing from an owner with a management or governance role, so some charter operators could not tap the program for their buildings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and targeted: money flows by formula and competitive grant to the districts with the worst buildings and the least ability to pay for repairs themselves, addressing conditions — bad air, lead in water, crumbling foundations — that directly affect children's health and learning. The cost is real and large: on the order of $100 billion in authorized spending plus $10 billion a year in tax-credit bond authority over five years, with cost-raising strings attached to every project. The bill is expensive but deliberately aimed at need rather than spread evenly.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in July 2023 and sat there with no hearing, markup, or floor vote for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Sen. Jack Reed introduced the Rebuild America's Schools Act on July 27, 2023, with 21 Senate Democrats joining as original sponsors.

The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, the committee that handles tax matters and would handle the bill's bond provisions; that referral was the last action recorded on the bill.
The bill finished the Congress with 23 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no further committee or floor action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No vote was ever forced, so no senator had to take a position. The federal treasury and state budgets avoided the new $100 billion commitment, while districts able to fund their own school buildings faced no new competition for aid; students in under-resourced schools got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal and state budgets; self-funding districts

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed
for.role: Senator from Rhode Island and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 23 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Democrat.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on July 27, 2023 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 cosponsors were Democrats — 23 of the Senate's 48 Democrats — no Republican signed on, and the bill died in a committee chaired by a Democrat without any recorded Republican action either.

industries.note: The bill would fund tens of billions of dollars a year of school repair and construction work, with federal prevailing-wage standards applying to bond-financed projects. Its gain comes from work the public is paying for, so the industry's interest in the bill runs alongside students' and communities'.

industries.industry: U.S. iron, steel, and construction-product manufacturers
industries.note: Projects must use domestically produced iron, steel, and manufactured products, with a waiver available only if domestic sourcing raises costs more than 25% or is unavailable. This channels the program's spending toward domestic producers.

The bill restores and creates federal tax-credit bonds that pay holders a credit covering 100% of district interest costs — a federal subsidy routed to investors in exchange for cheaper school construction financing. The public gets buildings; investors get a guaranteed federally backed return.
The bill bars any funds from going to facilities of for-profit charter operators or charters leasing from an owner with a governance role, excluding them from a new source of construction money.
New construction must be certified under one of several named green rating systems, making private certification a required step in publicly funded school projects.
